title: Processes and Communication
tagline: Programs that start, watch and talk to each other on Windows
description: How separate programs on one Windows machine cooperate: what a process is, starting and supervising them, job objects, standard streams, anonymous and named pipes, message framing, serving many clients, overlapped I/O, shared memory with file mappings, ring buffers and seqlocks, named events, mutexes and semaphores, window messages between programs, deadlocks, local sockets, protocol design and serialisation, and securing it all. It ends with single-instance apps, worker processes, out-of-process plugins and a full client and server. It assumes the C++ course and the first milestones of the Win32 API course.

milestones.title: Processes
milestones.blurb: What a process is, starting one with the right environment, folder and handles, waiting for it and reading its exit code, job objects, talking through standard streams, and choosing between the ways programs can communicate.

lessons.title: What a Process Is
lessons.summary: A process is a running program's container - a private address space, a table of handles, a security token, one or more threads and an exit code. Process IDs and handles, why processes cannot see each other's memory, and why that isolation is the reason inter-process communication needs special tools.

lessons.title: Starting Processes Well
lessons.summary: Everything that goes into a new process besides its command line - the environment block and how to build one, the working directory, which handles it inherits and how to limit them to exactly the ones you mean, and the creation flags that matter.

lessons.title: Waiting, Exit Codes and Jobs
lessons.summary: Knowing how a child process ended - waiting with timeouts, exit code conventions and the NTSTATUS codes a crash leaves behind - and job objects that group processes, end them all at once and limit what they can use.

lessons.title: Talking Through Standard Streams
lessons.summary: The simplest channel between a parent and a child - its standard input, output and error redirected to pipes - and the deadlocks waiting for anyone who reads them carelessly, plus line-based protocols over stdio as used by language servers and many tools.

lessons.title: Choosing an IPC Method
lessons.summary: A map of the ways processes communicate on Windows - pipes, shared memory, sockets, kernel objects, window messages, files, COM and RPC - compared on speed, simplicity, who can connect and what happens when one side dies, with a guide to choosing.

projects.title: Running a compiler from an editor

milestones.title: Pipes
milestones.blurb: Anonymous pipes, named pipes between unrelated programs, framing messages on a byte stream, serving many clients at once, and overlapped I/O with completion ports.

lessons.title: Anonymous Pipes
lessons.summary: The one-way byte channel behind standard streams - creating a pipe, its buffer and what happens when it fills, end-of-file and broken pipes, peeking without blocking, and passing pipe ends to a child.

tasks.title: A pipe that behaves like the real one

lessons.title: Named Pipes
lessons.summary: Pipes any program can find by name - creating a server instance, waiting for a client to connect, connecting as a client and handling a busy server, byte and message modes, disconnecting, and the rules for pipe names.

lessons.title: Message Framing
lessons.summary: Turning a byte stream into messages - length prefixes and why they beat delimiters for binary data, choosing the size and byte order of the length, refusing absurd lengths, reading exactly N bytes, and recovering when the other side sends nonsense.

lessons.title: Serving Many Clients
lessons.summary: A pipe server that handles several clients at once - one instance per client, the accept loop with a thread per connection, keeping an instance always listening, identifying who connected, limits, and shutting the server down cleanly.

lessons.title: Overlapped I/O and Completion Ports
lessons.summary: Doing pipe I/O without blocking a thread per operation - FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, OVERLAPPED structures and events, ERROR_IO_PENDING, GetOverlappedResult, and I/O completion ports that let a few threads serve thousands of connections as state machines.

tasks.title: A connection as a state machine

milestones.title: Shared Memory
milestones.blurb: File mappings that two processes see at once, laying out data that works at any address, lock-free ring buffers, memory-mapped files, and seqlocks for publishing snapshots.

lessons.title: File Mappings
lessons.summary: Shared memory on Windows - a named file mapping backed by the page file, views mapped into each process at different addresses, sizes and page rounding, Local and Global names, who creates and who opens, and when the memory goes away.

lessons.title: Laying Out Shared Data
lessons.summary: What may live in shared memory and what may not - offsets instead of pointers, fixed-size types instead of std::string and std::vector, a header with a magic number, version and size, safe initialisation when either side may start first, and lock-free atomics.

tasks.title: A list that works at any address

lessons.title: Ring Buffers
lessons.summary: A queue in shared memory without locks - a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer with a write counter and a read counter, power-of-two capacities, detecting full and empty, acquire and release ordering, and what to do when the buffer is full.

lessons.title: Memory-Mapped Files
lessons.summary: Mapping a real file into memory - reading huge files as if they were arrays, views of part of a file and the 64 KB granularity rule, writing through a mapping and flushing it, growing a mapped file, sharing a mapped file between processes, and the errors that arrive as exceptions.

lessons.title: Seqlocks and Snapshots
lessons.summary: Publishing a state that changes constantly, such as a game's player positions for an external tool - why readers can see torn data, double buffering, and the seqlock - a sequence counter that lets readers detect a write in progress and retry without ever blocking the writer.

projects.title: A message ring in shared memory

milestones.title: Synchronisation Across Processes
milestones.blurb: Named events, mutexes and semaphores, waiting on several things at once, abandoned mutexes when a process dies, window messages between programs, and avoiding deadlocks.

lessons.title: Named Kernel Objects
lessons.summary: Events, mutexes and semaphores that several processes can open by name - creating versus opening, ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS, the session namespaces, signalled and non-signalled states, and why a kernel object outlives the handle that made it until the last handle closes.

lessons.title: Events and Waiting
lessons.summary: Signalling between processes with events - auto-reset versus manual-reset, SetEvent and ResetEvent, the lost-wakeup trap and how to avoid it, WaitForMultipleObjects for waiting on several things at once, and the return values every wait must check.

tasks.title: Auto-reset, manual-reset and waiting for several

lessons.title: Mutexes, Semaphores and Abandonment
lessons.summary: Exclusive access across processes with a named mutex - ownership, recursion, releasing, and WAIT_ABANDONED when the owner died holding it - and semaphores for limiting how many can do something at once.

lessons.title: Window Messages Between Programs
lessons.summary: Programs with windows can talk through messages - finding another program's window, WM_COPYDATA for sending a block of data, registered message numbers, message-only windows, SendMessage versus PostMessage, and the privilege boundary UIPI puts in the way.

lessons.title: Deadlocks and Timeouts
lessons.summary: How cooperating processes get stuck waiting for each other - lock-order deadlocks, request-reply deadlocks over pipes, waiting for a peer that died - and the disciplines that prevent them - a global lock order, timeouts on every wait, never holding a lock across IPC, and watchdogs.

milestones.title: Local Sockets and Protocols
milestones.blurb: Sockets on one machine, designing a message protocol, serialising data so both sides agree, requests, responses and events, and securing local communication against other programs.

lessons.title: Sockets on One Machine
lessons.summary: Using sockets for local IPC - Winsock start-up, a TCP server bound to 127.0.0.1 and never to every interface, letting the system choose a port and publishing it in a file, Unix domain sockets on Windows, and how sockets compare with named pipes.

lessons.title: Designing a Message Protocol
lessons.summary: The decisions behind a protocol two programs will speak for years - a handshake with a magic number and version, an envelope with type, id, flags and length, kinds of messages, version negotiation, error replies, and writing it all down.

lessons.title: Serialising Data
lessons.summary: Turning values into bytes both sides read the same way - fixed-width little-endian numbers, length-prefixed UTF-8 strings, variable-length integers and zigzag encoding, tag-length-value records that let new fields be added without breaking old readers, and when to use JSON or a library instead.

lessons.title: Requests, Responses and Events
lessons.summary: The flow of a conversation - request ids that match responses to requests, many requests in flight at once, timeouts and cancellation, events the server sends unasked, what ordering a stream does and does not guarantee, and safe retries.

lessons.title: Securing Local Communication
lessons.summary: Local IPC is an attack surface - other users, other programs and even web pages can reach it. Access control on pipes and objects, preventing pipe squatting, checking which program you are talking to, tokens for localhost sockets, the Host header against DNS rebinding, validating every message, and the dangers of impersonation.

milestones.title: Building Real Systems
milestones.blurb: Single-instance applications, supervised worker processes, plugins in their own processes, testing and debugging communication, and a complete client and server.

lessons.title: A Single-Instance Application
lessons.summary: Making a second launch hand its work to the copy already running - a named mutex to detect the first instance, forwarding the command line through a pipe or WM_COPYDATA, resolving relative paths with the sender's folder, bringing the window to the front, and the races when two copies start at once.

lessons.title: Worker Processes
lessons.summary: Doing work in separate processes on purpose - isolating crashes, using several cores, running with fewer rights - and the supervisor that starts workers, watches their heartbeats, restarts them with exponential backoff, and stops trying when they keep crashing.

lessons.title: Plugins in Separate Processes
lessons.summary: Running extensions out of process, as editors and browsers do - the host and plugin protocol, manifests and API version compatibility, subscribing plugins to events, timeouts for slow plugins, disabling misbehaving ones, and what isolation does and does not protect.

lessons.title: Testing and Debugging IPC
lessons.summary: Making communicating programs testable - keeping the protocol logic separate from the transport, in-memory transports and fault injection, golden transcripts, logging both sides with ids and times, and the tools for seeing handles, pipes and traffic, including debugging two processes at once.

lessons.title: Case Studies
lessons.summary: How real systems combine the techniques of this course - a multi-process browser, an editor and its language servers, a game and its live editor link, a Windows service with a tray application - and the questions to ask when designing your own.
